name: Domaine Pierre Usseglio & Fils Châteauneuf-du-Pape Réserve des Deux Frères 2015
text:
## Domaine Pierre Usseglio & Fils Châteauneuf-du-Pape Réserve des Deux Frères 2015

### The region

[Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chateauneuf-du-Pape,+Vaucluse,+France&t=k) sits in the southern Rhône, between Orange and [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Avignon,+Vaucluse,+France&t=k). Eighteen grape varieties are permitted by law, and most wines blend some of them; for reds, Grenache leads, with Mourvèdre and Syrah usually next in line.

The village is named for the "new castle of the Pope," built when the papacy lived in Avignon. The ruined keep, the [Château des Papes](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chateau+des+Papes,+Chateauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k), still stands over the village, and it shows up well from above.

### The producer

The domaine began in 1948, when the Italian immigrant Francis Usseglio bought twenty acres in the southern Rhône and made his own wine the following year. Francis had two sons, Pierre and Raymond. One account dates Domaine Pierre Usseglio itself to 1966, when Pierre took over his father's estate and Raymond left to start his own domaine. Sources differ slightly on that date. Pierre's children have run the estate since 1999.

The "two brothers" in the name are Pierre's sons, Thierry and Jean-Pierre. They gradually modernized the winemaking and bought another eight hectares of very old vines. That purchase is what made the Deux Frères bottling possible. Its first vintage was 2000. The estate holds 24 hectares in Châteauneuf, spread over 17 small parcels.

This is a rare wine. Réserve des Deux Frères isn't made every year, and when it is, production is only about 500 cases. One writer adds a practical warning: the bottles are oversized and won't fit standard wine racks. Jon may already know this.

### The grapes

For 2015, Jeb Dunnuck reports that the wine is 100% Grenache, aged in a mix of new and once-used barrels (60%). The Wine Advocate describes the oak differently: barriques, one-third of them new. Either way, this is a more oak-influenced and modern style than many traditional Châteauneufs, which are aged in large old foudres.

Some retail listings show a Grenache–Mourvèdre–Syrah blend for this wine. That appears to be a generic description. In other years the blend does vary: the 2020 adds a little very old-vine Serine (an old Syrah strain) from Charbonnière.

### What the critics say (2015 vintage)

**Jeb Dunnuck, 96 points (2015, bottle review).** Dunnuck found the 2015 more closed and structured than the estate's other top cuvée. He describes dark fruit, smoky herbs, savoury roasted-meat and licorice tones, with whole-cluster stems well absorbed by the fruit. He praises its concentration, texture and fresh acidity. He advised waiting 4–5 years, then drinking over the following 15–20.

**Jeb Dunnuck for robertparker.com, 95–97 points (2015, barrel sample, October 2016).** The earlier barrel review was in the same range. It called the wine inky and massively layered, modern in style but still clearly southern Rhône, with sweet tannins and good balance.

**The Wine Advocate, 94 points (2015).** This reviewer liked the creamy richness, concentration and length. He was a little more reserved about the obvious oak and the alcoholic warmth. That review is reprinted by Benchmark Wine Cellar.

**Merchant view.** UK merchant Uncorked, offering the 2015s in 2017, rated both reserve bottlings, Mon Aïeul and Deux Frères, as outstanding.

**CellarTracker community.** I couldn't open the CellarTracker page for the 2015, so I can't confirm the community notes myself. The 95.67 in your list comes from your family's cellar data, and I haven't verified it independently.

### The vintage

Louis Barruol of Château St-Cosme called 2015 a major vintage, with the Grenache better than in 2013 or 2014 and the wines not as hot as 2001 or 2003. Decanter noted that Grenache ripened slowly in the cooler northern parts of the appellation, while alcohol could run high in the warmer south. Growers with old-vine Grenache and Mourvèdre made the best wines. That suits this cuvée exactly.

### A curious aside: the stones

The famous Châteauneuf soil is the galets roulés. These are large, rounded stones, mostly quartzite, carried down and smoothed by the ancient Rhône. At many sites they lie on the surface over layers of clay, sand and limestone. The stones help moderate soil temperature, and the sandy layers drain freely.

The common story is that the stones soak up heat by day and release it at night. Like any thermal mass, they mostly smooth out temperature swings. Whatever the exact mechanism, they help Grenache ripen fully, which is part of why 15.5% alcohol is normal here.

### Practical note

**Drink now or cellar:** At 11 years old, the 2015 is now in Dunnuck's suggested window, which runs to about 2035–2040. It's a good time to open one. If Jon has several bottles, there is no hurry with the rest.

**Decant:** Yes, for about an hour. That helps the oak and the 15.5% alcohol settle, and it lets the bottle's sediment drop. Serve it slightly cool. One guide suggests about 15.5 °C (60 °F) for this producer's wines, for freshness and lift.

**Food:** Braised lamb shoulder with rosemary and garlic, a Provençal beef daube, or duck confit with lentils. The roasted-meat and garrigue notes match slow-cooked, herb-scented dishes. Avoid anything very spicy, because heat in the food makes high alcohol feel hotter.

### From the history books

- **1309–1377, the Avignon Papacy:** The popes lived at Avignon for most of the 14th century. Pope John XXII built the summer castle that gave Châteauneuf-du-Pape its name. [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Avignon+Papacy&go=Go) · [Pope John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Pope+John+XXII&go=Go)
- **1923–1936, the first appellation rules:** Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié of [Château Fortia](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chateau+Fortia,+Chateauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) led the local growers in drawing up production rules in 1923. Those rules became the model for France's appellation system, and Châteauneuf-du-Pape was recognized as an AOC in 1936. [Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Pierre+Le+Roy+de+Boiseaumari%C3%A9&go=Go) · [Châteauneuf-du-Pape AOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape+AOC&go=Go)
- **1948, an immigrant's start:** Francis Usseglio, one of many Italians who came to work the vineyards of southern France, bought his first vines that year (see the producer section). [Italian immigration to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Italian+immigration+to+France&go=Go)

1. Domaine Pierre Usseglio & Fils Châteauneuf-du-Pape Réserve des Deux Frères 2015 — from Jon's cellar (no price listed), 750 ml — 96 points, Jeb Dunnuck, 2015 vintage (bottle review). The Wine Advocate gave the 2015 94.
